translationRepairs: At the time the headquarters Registrar Zong Xie also had lofty tastes; Daogui and both men alike looked to one another for a life beyond official business.
At the time the headquarters Registrar Zong Xie also had lofty tastes; Daogui counted on both men alike for companionship beyond official business.
道規 is the subject of 並以事外相期: Daogui looked to both Jinghong and Zong Xie for extra-official companionship, not a three-way mutual gaze among all three.

The late Palace Attendant, Left Grand Master of the Palace, and Jinghong, who held the privilege of an office equal to the Three Excellencies, had a spirit unassuming and plain and a vision lofty and far-reaching. His virtue reached the capital's gate-towers, his Way enriched hill and garden alike.

The late Palace Attendant, Left Grand Master of the Palace with the privilege of an office equal to the Three Excellencies, Jinghong, had a spirit unassuming and plain and a vision lofty and far-reaching. His virtue reached the capital's gate-towers; his Way enriched hill and garden alike.
The Chinese strings three offices then the name 敬弘 (故侍中、左光祿大夫、開府儀同三司敬弘); the original English makes Jinghong a separate conjunct from 開府儀同三司.

The late Palace Attendant, Left Grand Master of the Palace, and Jinghong, who held the privilege of an office equal to the Three Excellencies, had a spirit and bearing unassuming and plain, understanding and scope lofty and steep; his virtue spread to the gate-towers of the capital, his Way enriched hill and garden.

The late Palace Attendant, Left Grand Master of the Palace, and holder of the privilege of an office equal to the Three Excellencies, Jinghong, had a spirit and bearing unassuming and plain, understanding and scope lofty and steep; his virtue spread to the gate-towers of the capital, his Way enriched hill and garden.
The same title string names Jinghong as the holder of 開府儀同三司; the original 'and Jinghong, who held' splits him off as a fourth item.
Jinghong was short in stature, yet in sitting and rising he was perfectly upright. Huan Xuan called him "the eight formations of go."
Jinghong was short in stature, yet in sitting and rising he was perfectly upright. Huan Xuan called him "the eight formations of tanqi."
彈棊 is tanqi (pellet chess), not 圍棋/go; Huan Xuan's epithet 彈棊八勢 is mistranslated.
Jinghong's form was short and small, yet in sitting and rising he was upright and square. Huan Xuan called him "the eight formations of go."
Jinghong's form was short and small, yet in sitting and rising he was upright and square. Huan Xuan called him "the eight formations of tanqi."
The literal field repeats the same 彈棊/go error; tanqi is the correct game name.

Xu Xiu of Donghai, He Tan of Lujiang, Huang Hui, Sun Zichang and Wang Yanxiu of Taiyuan, Kong Huixuan of Lu Commandery, and others all admired the Way and came to study; this was called the Southern School.

Xu Xiu of Donghai, He Tan of Lujiang, Huang Hui, Xun Zihua of Yingchuan, Sun Zongchang and Wang Yanxiu of Taiyuan, and Kong Huixuan of Lu Commandery all admired the Way and came to study; this was called the Southern School.
The proposal rightly restores 潁川荀子華 and 孫宗昌, but 並慕道來遊 names that closed list, not an open 'and others.'

The literal line needs the same name restorations and should not add 'and others' absent from the Chinese list.
When Emperor Shaodi came to the throne, Shangzhi became Advisory Army Aide on the Household Cavalry staff of the Prince of Luling, Yizhen.
When Emperor Shaodi came to the throne, Shangzhi became Advisory Army Aide to the Prince of Luling, Yizhen, General of Chariots and Cavalry.
車騎諮議參軍 is staff to the prince as 車騎將軍, not Household Cavalry; the proposal's 'as General of Chariots and Cavalry' can be read as Shangzhi's rank.

If limited to four or five zhu, the inscriptions are all ancient seal script, which common people do not recognize; moreover some are worn away and especially hard to distinguish. Public and private will be thrown into confusion and lawsuits will surely arise—this is his deepest doubt.

If limited to four or five zhu, the inscriptions are all ancient seal script, which I, your humble servant, do not recognize; moreover some are worn away and especially hard to distinguish. Public and private will be thrown into confusion and lawsuits will surely arise—this is the deepest of these doubts.
下走 is Shangzhi's humble self-reference, not a class of 'those in humble service'; 其深疑 marks this as the gravest of the doubts just listed.

In the twenty-ninth year he retired and at Fang Mountain wrote a Rhapsody on Retirement to declare what he upheld, but commentators all said Shangzhi could not hold firm to his resolve. Yuan Shu, Left Commander of the Heir Apparent's Guard, wrote to him: "Yesterday I sent inquiry and learned that you, sir, have hidden your will in mountain fields. Though one says the rites of age should be followed, this is hard to esteem so highly. Bi Shu, Ban Chao, Bing, and Wei would shine in former records; Gong, Gong, Shan, and Wei would sink in shame in past chapters.

In the twenty-ninth year he retired and at Fang Mountain wrote a Rhapsody on Retirement to declare what he upheld, but commentators all said Shangzhi could not hold firm to his resolve. Yuan Shu, Left Commander of the Heir Apparent's Guard, wrote to him: "Yesterday I sent inquiry and learned that you, sir, have hidden your will in mountain fields. Though one says the rites of age should be followed, this is hard to esteem so highly. Shu, Ban, Bing, and Wei would then share excellence in former records; Gong, Gong, Shan, and Wei would sink in shame in past chapters.
疎 is the surname Shu, not 'Bi Shu'; 班 is Ban; 俾疎、班、邴、魏，通美於前策 is a wish that they would share excellence in former records.
Shangzhi's residence was beside Nanjian Temple, hence the letter says 'southern bank'—as in the Mao Ode's 'To gather duckweed, on the southern stream's bank.'"
Shangzhi's residence was beside Nanjian Temple, hence the letter says 'southern bank'—as in the Mao Ode's 'To gather duckweed, on the southern stream's bank.'
The historian's gloss is not quoted speech; the extra closing quotation mark after the Mao Ode citation is stray.

Edicts earnestly urged him. The emperor also sent an edict to the Prince of Jiangxia, Yigong, saying, "Court worthies are few today, and Yang and Meng have not yet been permitted to retire. Shangzhi's appointment and favor are special—is it then not fitting to grant his request?"

Edicts earnestly urged him. The emperor also sent an edict to the Prince of Jiangxia, Yigong, saying, "Court worthies are few today, and Yang and Meng have not yet been permitted to retire. Shangzhi's appointment and favor are special—so it is not yet fitting to grant his request, is it?"
After 羊、孟尚不得告謝, 便未宜申許邪 asks for agreement that Shangzhi too should not yet be allowed to retire; the original English reads as urging the grant.
His son Shao married the sixteenth daughter of Emperor Taizu, the Princess of Nan Commandery; his daughter married the Prince of Pengcheng, Yikang, and the Lamented Prince of Baling, Xiuruo.
His son Shao married the sixteenth daughter of Emperor Taizu, the Princess of Nan Commandery; his daughters married the Prince of Pengcheng, Yikang, and the Lamented Prince of Baling, Xiuruo.
女適彭城王義康、巴陵哀王休若 records two marriages and therefore two daughters, not one woman married to both princes.
Qingzhi repeatedly declined ennoblement; the court earnestly urged him with great sincerity. Shangzhi said to him, "The sovereign empties his mind and sits sidewise—how could you firmly decline?"

Qingzhi repeatedly declined ennoblement; the court earnestly urged him with great sincerity. Shangzhi said to him, "The sovereign opens his mind and keeps a seat at his side—how could you firmly decline?"
虛懷側席 is the ruler's open mind and a vacant side seat for a worthy, not sitting 'sidewise.'

He was on good terms with Wang Wei of Langye. When Youzhi died, Wei wrote to Yan: "I and the Administrator of Yixing only regret that we knew each other late; I always thought that a gentleman understood me.

The silent subject of 與琅邪王微相善 continues 悠之 from the previous sentence; naming Youzhi prevents assigning the friendship to Shangzhi or Yan.
